{{Short description|Japanese noble family which ruled as a shogunate from 1603 to 1867}} {{Japanese clan name |surname = Tokugawa |surname nihongo = 徳川 |image = Mitsubaaoi.svg |image size=200px |caption = Tokugawa clan [[Mon (emblem)|mon]] |province of origin ={{Plainlist| * {{ill|Mikawa Province|en|Mikawa Province|WD=Q768158|lt=Mikawa|1=Mikawa Province}}}} |parent house ={{Plainlist| * [[Minamoto clan]] * {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta clan|1=Nitta clan}} (Via a female member via marriage) * {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira clan|1=Matsudaira clan}}}} |titles =Various |founder ={{Plainlist| * {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}}} |final ruler =[[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] |current head ={{ill|Iehiro Tokugawa|en|Iehiro Tokugawa|WD=Q7004131|lt=Iehiro Tokugawa|1=Iehiro Tokugawa}} |year start =[[1567]] |year end =[[1868]] |founding year ={{Plainlist| * 1567}} |ruled until ={{Plainlist| * 1868 (abolition of the shogunate) * 1871 ({{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}})}} |cadet branches = Various, including * ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'': **[[:en:Owari-Tokugawa family|Owari-Tokugawa family]] **[[:en:Kishū-Tokugawa family|Kishū-Tokugawa family]], with 3 cadet branches ''{{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Gosankyō|1=Gosankyō}}'': ***Tayasu family ***Hitotsubashi family ***Shimizu family **[[:en:Mito-Tokugawa family|Mito-Tokugawa family]] ***Matsudo-Tokugawa family ***{{ill|Tokugawa Yoshinobu family|en|Tokugawa Yoshinobu family|WD=Q7480630|lt=Tokugawa Yoshinobu family|1=Tokugawa Yoshinobu family}} }}
The '''Tokugawa clan''' (''{{ill|Shinjitai|en|Shinjitai|WD=Q1055887|lt=Shinjitai|1=Shinjitai}}'': 徳川氏, ''{{ill|Kyūjitai|en|Kyūjitai|WD=Q1147857|lt=Kyūjitai|1=Kyūjitai}}'': 德川氏, ''Tokugawa-shi'' or ''Tokugawa-uji'') is a Japanese dynasty which produced the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa shoguns]] who ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868 during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. It was formerly a powerful ''[[Daimyo|daimyō]]'' family. They nominally descended from {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|en|Emperor Seiwa|WD=Q349243|lt=Emperor Seiwa|1=Emperor Seiwa}} (850–880) and were a branch of the [[Minamoto clan]] ({{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji|1=Seiwa Genji}}) through the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira clan|1=Matsudaira clan}}. The early history of the clan remains a mystery.<ref name="aichi">{{cite web |url=http://www.aichi-pref-library.jp/chiki/jyousetsu_7.html |script-title=ja:徳川家康展 |publisher=Aichi Prefectural Library |access-date=2008-12-28 |language=ja |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050419182453/http://www.aichi-pref-library.jp/chiki/jyousetsu_7.html |archive-date=2005-04-19 }}</ref> Nominally, the Matsudaira clan is said to be descended from the {{ill|Nitta clan|en|Nitta clan|WD=Q2274150|lt=Nitta clan|1=Nitta clan}}, a branch of the Minamoto clan, but the likelihood of this claim is considered quite low or untrue.<ref name="kototoku">{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%B3%E5%B7%9D%E6%B0%8F-104688|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230629141133/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%B3%E5%B7%9D%E6%B0%8F-104688|script-title=ja:徳川氏|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|date=|archive-date=29 June 2023|access-date=29 June 2023}}</ref><ref name="jktoku">{{cite web|url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230319132621/https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2026|script-title=ja:徳川氏|language=ja|publisher=Japan Knowledge|date=|archive-date=19 March 2023|access-date=23 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="nj230324">{{cite web|url=https://www.touken-world.jp/tips/103914/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240323132440/https://www.touken-world.jp/tips/103914/|script-title=ja:松平元康はなぜ徳川家康になったのか|language=ja|publisher=The Nagoya Japanese Sword Museum Nagoya Touken world|date=|archive-date=23 March 2024|access-date=23 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="re230324">{{cite web|url=https://www.rekishijin.com/21007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328183748/https://www.rekishijin.com/21007|script-title=ja:徳川家康は源氏の英雄・源義家の子孫にあたるのか？|language=ja|publisher=Rekishijin|date=|archive-date=28 March 2023|access-date=23 March 2024}}</ref>
==History== {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshishige|en|Minamoto no Yoshishige|WD=Q732097|lt=Minamoto no Yoshishige|1=Minamoto no Yoshishige}} (1135–1202), grandson of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|en|Minamoto no Yoshiie|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie|1=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} (1041–1108), was the first to take the name of Nitta. He sided with his cousin [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] against the [[Taira clan]] (1180) and accompanied him to {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}. Nitta Yoshisue, 4th son of Yoshishige, settled at Tokugawa (Kozuke province) and took the name of that place. Their provincial history book did not mention Minamoto clan or Nitta clan.<ref name="okazaki">{{cite web|url=http://www.city.okazaki.aichi.jp/museum/db/kkp/H12-09-15/ky00401.htm|script-title=ja:十四松平の城・寺・墓を訪ねて|publisher=[[Okazaki, Aichi|Okazaki]]|year=2000|access-date=2008-12-27|language=ja|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090114031034/http://www.city.okazaki.aichi.jp/museum/db/kkp/H12-09-15/ky00401.htm|archive-date=2009-01-14}}</ref>
The nominal originator of the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira clan|1=Matsudaira clan}} was reportedly {{ill|Matsudaira Chikauji|en|Matsudaira Chikauji|WD=Q11239169|lt=Matsudaira Chikauji|1=Matsudaira Chikauji}}, who was originally a poor Buddhist monk.<ref name="aichi" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.shinchosha.co.jp/books/html/115244.html|title=Ieyasu Tokugawa|publisher=Shinchosha|author=Ryōtarō Shiba|author-link=Ryōtarō Shiba|year=1962|access-date=2008-12-29|language=ja|archive-date=2008-11-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081102025202/http://www.shinchosha.co.jp/books/html/115244.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He reportedly descended from Nitta Yoshisue in the 8th generation and witnessed the ruin of the Nitta in their war against the {{ill|Ashikaga clan|en|Ashikaga clan|WD=Q725370|lt=Ashikaga|1=Ashikaga clan}}. He settled at Matsudaira (Mikawa province) and was adopted by his wife's family. Their provincial history book claimed that this original clan was Ariwara clan.<ref name="okazaki" /> Because this place is said to have been reclaimed by Ariwara Nobumori, one theory holds that Matsudaira clan was related to {{ill|Ariwara no Narihira|en|Ariwara no Narihira|WD=Q451991|lt=Ariwara no Narihira|1=Ariwara no Narihira}}.<ref>{{in lang|ja}} Kazue Tanaka. [https://books.google.com/books?id=944KovAOCd0C&pg=PA101 古代史の謎を解き明かす「モード・タ」]. ''{{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}}''. via Bungeisha. 2000. 101.</ref>
Matsudaira Nobumitsu (15th century), son of Chikauji, was in charge of {{ill|Okazaki Castle|en|Okazaki Castle|WD=Q1013445|lt=Okazaki Castle|1=Okazaki Castle}}, and strengthened the authority of his family in the Mikawa province. Nobumitsu's great-great-grandson [[Matsudaira Kiyoyasu]] made his clan strong, but was assassinated. In 1567, Matsudaira Motonobu—then known as {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} (1542–1616)—grandson of Kiyoyasu, was recognized by {{ill|Emperor Ōgimachi|en|Emperor Ōgimachi|WD=Q334076|lt=Emperor Ōgimachi|1=Emperor Ōgimachi}} as a descendant of {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji|1=Seiwa Genji}}; he also started the family name Tokugawa. According to historical documents from the same period, some of the three generations of the Matsudaira clan, including Nobumitsu, took the surname Kamo no Ason (Kamo) , and the Matsudaira clan's hollyhock crest also suggests a connection to the Kamo clan, so some have pointed out that they were actually vassals of the Kamo clan.{{sfn|Kasatani |1997 |p=36}} Tokugawa Ieyasu himself signed the letter of assurance to the Suganuma clan in 1561, shortly after independence from the Imagawa clan, as "Minamoto no Motoyasu" ("Suganuma Family Genealogy" and "Documents Possessed by Kunozan Toshogu Shrine")<ref>{{cite book |title=静岡県史〈資料編：中世3〉 |trans-title=Shizuoka Prefecture History (Reference Materials: Middle Ages 3) |date=1994 |page=1102 |url=https://www.book61.co.jp/book.php/N63325 |access-date=25 June 2024 |language=Ja}}{{cite book |title=『愛知県史〈織豊1〉|trans-title=Aichi Prefecture History (Oda-Toyotomi 1) |date=2003 |publisher=愛知県 |page=61 |url=https://www.book61.co.jp/book.php/N76979 |access-date=25 June 2024}}</ref>
The clan rose to power at the end of the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}. as their political influences and territories they controlled expanded during this period, they developed many new offices such as many magistrate official such as {{ill|Kōriki Kiyonaga|en|Kōriki Kiyonaga|WD=Q4352879|lt=Kōriki Kiyonaga|1=Kōriki Kiyonaga}}, {{ill|Amano Yasukage|en|Amano Yasukage|WD=Q4352847|lt=Amano Yasukage|1=Amano Yasukage}}, {{ill|Honda Shigetsugu|en|Honda Shigetsugu|WD=Q4346047|lt=Honda Shigetsugu|1=Honda Shigetsugu}}, and many others, to control their new territories and vassals.<ref name="Hamada Kōichirō Ieyasu vassals">{{cite web |author1=Hamada Kōichirō (濱田浩一郎) |author2=Rekishijin Editorial Department |title=三河一向一揆の鎮圧後、徳川家康はなぜ離反した家臣に寛大だったのか？ |trans-title=After suppressing the Mikawa Ikko Ikki uprising, why was Tokugawa Ieyasu lenient towards his defecting retainers? |url=https://www.rekishijin.com/26838 |website=Rekishijin |publisher=ABC ARC, inc. |access-date=24 June 2024 |language=Ja |date=2023 |quote=From "The Truth About Tokugawa Ieyasu" in the February 2023 issue of Rekishijin article}}</ref> In 1566, as Ieyasu declared his independence from the Imagawa clan, he reformed the order of Mikawa province starting with the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira clan|1=Matsudaira clan}}, after he pacified {{ill|Mikawa Province|en|Mikawa Province|WD=Q768158|lt=Mikawa|1=Mikawa Province}}. This decision was made after he counseled by his senior vassal {{ill|Sakai Tadatsugu|en|Sakai Tadatsugu|WD=Q1132756|lt=Sakai Tadatsugu|1=Sakai Tadatsugu}} to abandon their allegiance with the Imagawa clan.<ref>{{harvtxt|Arthur Lindsay Sadler |2014|p=57}}</ref> He also strengthened his powerbase by creating a military government system of Tokugawa clan in Mikawa which based from his hereditary vassals {{ill|Fudai daimyō|en|Fudai daimyō|WD=Q643640|lt=Fudai daimyō|1=Fudai daimyō}}. The system which called "''Sanbi no gunsei''" (三備の軍制) with the structure divide the governance into three sections:<ref>{{cite book |author1=Tamotsu Fujino |title=徳川政権と幕閣 |trans-title=Tokugawa government and Bakufu |date=1995 |publisher=新人物往来社 |location=11 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SYINAQAAMAAJ |access-date=27 May 2024 |language=Ja}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Tamotsu Fujino |title=徳川幕閣: 武功派と官僚派の抗争 |trans-title=Tokugawa Shogunate: Conflict between the military faction and the bureaucratic faction |date=1967 |publisher=中央公論社 |pages=16, 29 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DnJDAAAAYAAJ |access-date=27 May 2024 |language=Ja}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Rizō Takeuchi |title=角川日本地名大辞典: 愛知県 |trans-title= |date=1978 |publisher=Kadokawa Shoten |page=41 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZgMRAQAAMAAJ |access-date=27 May 2024 |language=Ja}}</ref>
# {{ill|Hatamoto|en|Hatamoto|WD=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto|1=Hatamoto}}-Senshi: Ieyasu's direct vassals unit of army. Their task was to personally protect Ieyasu, the earliest commanders of this unit such as Matsudaira Ietada (Tojo), {{ill|Torii Mototada|en|Torii Mototada|WD=Q665518|lt=Torii Mototada|1=Torii Mototada}}, {{ill|Honda Tadakatsu|en|Honda Tadakatsu|WD=Q467417|lt=Honda Tadakatsu|1=Honda Tadakatsu}}, {{ill|Sakakibara Yasumasa|en|Sakakibara Yasumasa|WD=Q1062738|lt=Sakakibara Yasumasa|1=Sakakibara Yasumasa}}, {{ill|Ōkubo Tadayo|en|Ōkubo Tadayo|WD=Q869401|lt=Ōkubo Tadayo|1=Ōkubo Tadayo}}, Osuga Yasutaka, Uomura Iezumi, and others # Higashi Mikawa: unit of Western Mikawa province army, put under the control of Sakai Tadatsugu as overall commander, the commanders of this unit consisted of many Matsudaira clansmen and other hereditary vassals of Tokugawa such as {{ill|Matsudaira Ietada (Fukōzu)|en|Matsudaira Ietada (Fukōzu)|WD=Q6788035|lt=Matsudaira Ietada (Fukōzu)|1=Matsudaira Ietada (Fukōzu)}}, {{ill|Matsudaira Tadamasa|en|Matsudaira Tadamasa|WD=Q2814515|lt=Matsudaira Tadamasa|1=Matsudaira Tadamasa}}, {{ill|Matsudaira Ietada (Katahara)|en|Matsudaira Ietada (Katahara)|WD=Q11239164|lt=Matsudaira Ietada (Katahara)|1=Matsudaira Ietada (Katahara)}}, and others # Nishi-Mikawa: unit of Eastern Mikawa province army, put under the control of Ishikawa Ienari (De jure, De facto was his nephew, [[Ishikawa Kazumasa]]) as overall commander, the commanders of this unit consisted of many Matsudaira clansmen and other hereditary vassals which assigned on eastern side of the province, such as Shimada Heizo, {{ill|Hiraiwa Chikayoshi|en|Hiraiwa Chikayoshi|WD=Q849070|lt=Hiraiwa Chikayoshi|1=Hiraiwa Chikayoshi}}, [[Naitō Ienaga]], {{ill|Sakai Tadatoshi|en|Sakai Tadatoshi|WD=Q11644106|lt=Sakai Tadatoshi|1=Sakai Tadatoshi}}, Matsudaira Shinichi, and others.
To the end of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} they ruled Japan as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}s''. During the Edo period There were fifteen [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa ''shoguns'']]. Their dominance was so strong that some history books use the term "Tokugawa era" instead of "Edo period". Their principal family shrine is the {{ill|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|en|Nikkō Tōshō-gū|WD=Q696641|lt=Tōshō-gū|1=Nikkō Tōshō-gū}} in {{ill|Nikkō|en|Nikkō|WD=Q235753|lt=Nikkō|1=Nikkō}}, and their principal temples (''{{ill|Bodaiji|en|Bodaiji|WD=Q1084697|lt=Bodaiji|1=Bodaiji}}'') are [[Kan'ei-ji]] and {{ill|Zōjō-ji|en|Zōjō-ji|WD=Q249139|lt=Zōjō-ji|1=Zōjō-ji}}, both in {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Heirlooms of the clan are partly administered by the {{ill|Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|en|Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|WD=Q6584256|lt=Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|1=Tokugawa Memorial Foundation}}.
After the death of Ieyasu, in 1636, the heads of the ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'' (the three branches with {{ill|Han system|en|Han system|WD=Q841985|lt=fiefs|1=Han system}} in {{ill|Owari Province|en|Owari Province|WD=Q514506|lt=Owari|1=Owari Province}}, {{ill|Kii Province|en|Kii Province|WD=Q864053|lt=Kishū|1=Kii Province}}, and [[Mito, Ibaraki|Mito]]) also bore the Tokugawa surname, so did the three additional branches, known as the ''{{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Gosankyō|1=Gosankyō}}'': the Tayasu (1731), Hitotsubashi (1735), and Shimizu (1758) family, after the ascension of {{ill|Tokugawa Yoshimune|en|Tokugawa Yoshimune|WD=Q319664|lt=Tokugawa Yoshimune|1=Tokugawa Yoshimune}}. Once a {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}} died without a living heir, both the heads of ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'' (except [[:en:Mito-Tokugawa family|Mito-Tokugawa family]]) and ''{{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Gosankyō|1=Gosankyō}}'' had priority to succeed his position.<ref name="inj">Iwanami Nihonshi Jiten, ''Tokugawa Gosanke'', ''Tokugawa Owari-ke'', ''Tokugawa Kii-ke'', and ''Tokugawa Mito-ke''</ref><ref>Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Gosan-kyō''" in [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA882&dq= ''Japan encyclopedia'', p. 259]; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File].</ref> Many ''daimyōs'' descended from cadet branches of the clan, however, retained the surname {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|WD=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira|1=Matsudaira clan}}; examples include the Matsudaira of {{ill|Fukui Domain|en|Fukui Domain|WD=Q903537|lt=Fukui|1=Fukui Domain}} and {{ill|Aizu|en|Aizu|WD=Q1205071|lt=Aizu|1=Aizu}}. Members of the Tokugawa clan intermarried with prominent daimyo and the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Imperial|1=Emperor of Japan}} family.
On November 9, 1867, [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]], the 15th and the last shogun of Tokugawa, tendered his resignation to {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}. He formally stepped down ten days later, returning governing power to the Emperor,<ref>Takano Kiyoshi 高野澄 (1997). Tokugawa Yoshinobu: kindai Nihon no enshutsusha 德川慶喜 : 近代日本の演出者. (Tokyo: Nihon Hōsō Shuppan Kyōkai 日本放送出版協会), p. 256.</ref> marking the end of the ruling power of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]]. In 1868, {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|WD=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}} (1863–1940, from Tayasu family) was chosen as the heir to Yoshinobu as the head of Tokugawa clan.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ravina |first1=Mark |title=To Stand with the Nations of the World: Japan's Meiji Restoration in World History |date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0195327717}}</ref> On July 7, 1884, Iesato became a prince, just like the heads of some of other notable Japanese noble families, known as [[Kazoku]].<ref name="koshaku">{{cite book |title= 官報 |volume= 18840708 |number= 307 |chapter= 叙任 |page= 2 |url= http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2943511 |date= 1884-07-08 |access-date= 2018-07-24 |archive-date= 2022-01-20 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220120102732/https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2943511 |url-status= live }}[コマ番号2]。授公爵 従三位徳川家達</ref>
The 1946 {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|WD=Q237082|lt=Constitution of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}} abolished the ''kazoku'' and the noble titles, making Iesato's son, {{ill|Iemasa Tokugawa|en|Iemasa Tokugawa|WD=Q277171|lt=Iemasa Tokugawa|1=Iemasa Tokugawa}}, no longer a prince. Iemasa had a son Iehide, who died young, so he was succeeded by one of his grandsons, {{ill|Tsunenari Tokugawa|en|Tsunenari Tokugawa|WD=Q1131942|lt=Tsunenari|1=Tsunenari Tokugawa}}. Tsunenari is the second son of Toyoko (eldest daughter of Iemasa) and Ichirō Matsudaira (son of {{ill|Tsuneo Matsudaira|en|Tsuneo Matsudaira|WD=Q4121055|lt=Tsuneo Matsudaira|1=Tsuneo Matsudaira}}),<ref>{{cite book |last1=Satō |first1=Tomoyasu |title=門閥 — 旧華族階層の復権 |date=1987 |publisher=Rippu Shobo Publishing Co., Ltd. |isbn=978-4651700328 |pages=100, 105}}</ref> and he is also a patrilineal descendant of {{ill|Tokugawa Yorifusa|en|Tokugawa Yorifusa|WD=Q1133680|lt=Tokugawa Yorifusa|1=Tokugawa Yorifusa}}, the youngest son of Tokugawa Ieyasu.<ref>{{citation |url=http://reichsarchiv.jp/家系リスト/会津松平氏（御家門） |title=会津松平氏（御家門） |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190302024522/http://reichsarchiv.jp/%E5%AE%B6%E7%B3%BB%E3%83%AA%E3%82%B9%E3%83%88/%E4%BC%9A%E6%B4%A5%E6%9D%BE%E5%B9%B3%E6%B0%8F%EF%BC%88%E5%BE%A1%E5%AE%B6%E9%96%80%EF%BC%89 |archive-date=2019-03-02 |access-date=2019-09-09 }}</ref>
In 2007, Tsunenari published a book entitled Edo no idenshi (江戸の遺伝子), released in English in 2009 as The Edo Inheritance, which seeks to counter the common belief among Japanese that the Edo period was like a {{ill|Dark Ages (historiography)|en|Dark Ages (historiography)|WD=Q217192|lt=Dark Age|1=Dark Ages (historiography)}}, when Japan, {{ill|Sakoku|en|Sakoku|WD=Q332075|lt=cut off from the world|1=Sakoku}}, fell behind. On the contrary, he argues, the roughly 250 years of peace and relative prosperity saw great economic reforms, the growth of a sophisticated urban culture, and the development of the most urbanized society on the planet.<ref>"[http://www.i-house.or.jp/en/publications/ihousepress/theedoinheritance.html The Edo Inheritance by Tokugawa Tsunenari] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120219235501/http://www.i-house.or.jp/en/publications/ihousepress/theedoinheritance.html |date=2012-02-19 }}". International House of Japan. Retrieved 25 May 2009.</ref> Tsunenari formed the {{ill|Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|en|Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|WD=Q6584256|lt=Tokugawa Memorial Foundation|1=Tokugawa Memorial Foundation}} in 2003 to preserve and administer the historical objects, art, armor and documents that have been passed down in the Tokugawa family over the generations, display them for the general public and provide assistance to academic research on topics concerning historical Japan.
==Simplified descent== {{Tokugawa dynasty family tree}}
== Symbol == The Tokugawa's clan symbol, known in Japanese as a "[[Mon (emblem)|mon]]", the "triple {{ill|Alcea|en|Alcea|WD=Q1148371|lt=hollyhock|1=Alcea}}" (although commonly, but mistakenly identified as "hollyhock", the "aoi" actually belongs to the {{ill|Aristolochia|en|Aristolochia|WD=Q156212|lt=birthwort|1=Aristolochia}} family and translates as "{{ill|wild ginger|en|wild ginger|WD=Q8000918|lt=wild ginger|1=Wild ginger}}"—''Asarum''), has been a readily recognized icon in Japan, symbolizing in equal parts the Tokugawa clan and the last shogunate.
The symbol derives from a mythical clan, the Kamo clan, which legendarily descended from {{ill|Three-legged crow|en|Three-legged crow|WD=Q1323130|lt=Yatagarasu|1=Three-legged crow}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www4.ocn.ne.jp/~taxi/kamigamojinjya.html|script-title=ja:賀茂別雷神社|publisher=Kyoto sightseeing taxi|access-date=2008-12-30|language=ja|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090112091242/http://www4.ocn.ne.jp/~taxi/kamigamojinjya.html|archive-date=2009-01-12}}</ref> Matsudaira village was located in [[:en:Higashikamo District, Aichi|Higashikamo District]], {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}. Although {{ill|Emperor Go-Yōzei|en|Emperor Go-Yōzei|WD=Q349440|lt=Emperor Go-Yōzei|1=Emperor Go-Yōzei}} offered a new symbol, Ieyasu continued to use the symbol, which was not related to [[Minamoto clan]].<ref>{{in lang|ja}} Ryu Miura. [https://books.google.com/books?id=_UfeDjJO4G0C&pg=RA2-PA283 戦国武将・闇に消されたミステリー]. ''{{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}}''. via PHP Kenkyusho. 2005. 283.</ref>
In ''{{ill|Jidaigeki|en|Jidaigeki|WD=Q629917|lt=Jidaigeki|1=Jidaigeki}}'', the symbol is often shown to locate the story in the Edo period. In works set in during the [[Meiji Restoration]] movement, the symbol is used to show the bearer's allegiance to the shogunate—as opposed to the royalists, whose cause is symbolized by the Imperial throne's chrysanthemum symbol. Compare with the red and white rose iconography of English {{ill|Wars of the Roses|en|Wars of the Roses|WD=Q127751|lt=Wars of the Roses|1=Wars of the Roses}}, as imagined by {{ill|Walter Scott|en|Walter Scott|WD=Q79025|lt=Walter Scott|1=Walter Scott}} earlier in the 19th century, in ''{{ill|Anne of Geierstein|en|Anne of Geierstein|WD=Q2851345|lt=Anne of Geierstein|1=Anne of Geierstein}}'' (1829).
